title: Λέοντος βασιλεία
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 195. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων τις ἐβασίλευσεν οὐχὶ θυμώδης, οὐδὲ ὠμός, οὐδὲ βίαιος, ἀλλὰ πρᾷος καὶ δίκαιος, ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος.
sentences.tr: Leōn tis ebasileusen ouchi thymōdēs, oude ōmos, oude biaios, alla prāios kai dikaios, hōsper anthrōpos.
sentences.l: A certain lion came to reign, not hot-tempered, nor savage, nor violent, but gentle and just, like a human being.
sentences.n: ἐβασίλευσεν is an ingressive aorist — he came to the throne and held it. οὐχί is the emphatic form of οὐ, and the three negatives pile up so that the ἀλλά, when it comes, lands with weight. ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος: in a beast fable the highest compliment available is to say a lion behaved like a man.

sentences.t: Ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς αὐτοῦ βασιλείας συναθροισμὸς ἐγένετο πάντων τῶν ζῴων δοῦναι δίκας καὶ λαβεῖν πρὸς ἄλληλα, ὁ λύκος μὲν προβάτῳ, πάρδαλις δὲ αἰγάγρῳ, ἐλάφῳ δὲ τίγρις, κύων δὲ λαγωῷ.
sentences.tr: Epi de tēs autou basileias synathroismos egeneto pantōn tōn zōiōn dounai dikas kai labein pros allēla, ho lykos men probatōi, pardalis de aigagrōi, elaphōi de tigris, kyōn de lagōōi.
sentences.l: And in his reign an assembling came about of all the animals, to give satisfaction and to receive it from one another — the wolf to a sheep, the leopard to a wild goat, to a deer the tiger, and the dog to a hare.
sentences.i: In his reign all the animals came together to answer to one another at law and to obtain redress: the wolf to a sheep, the leopard to a wild goat, the tiger to a deer, the dog to a hare.
sentences.n: δίκας δοῦναι καὶ λαβεῖν is the standing legal idiom — to submit to judgement and to exact it, the whole business of a court in four words. Each dative names the party owed the satisfaction. Chambry's third pair reverses the order of the others, putting the injured deer before the tiger.

sentences.t: Ὁ πτὼξ δὲ ἔφη· « Πολλὰ ηὐχόμην ἰδεῖν τὴν ἡμέραν ταύτην, ἵνα τοῖς βιαίοις φοβερὰ τὰ εὐτελῆ φανῶσιν. »
sentences.tr: Ho ptōx de ephē· « Polla ēuchomēn idein tēn hēmeran tautēn, hina tois biaiois phobera ta eutelē phanōsin. »
sentences.l: And the hare said: « Much did I use to pray to see this day, so that to the violent the paltry creatures might appear fearful. »
sentences.i: And the hare said: « How often I prayed to see this day, so that the violent might find the small and cheap a thing to fear. »
sentences.n: πτώξ, 'the cowerer', is a poetic name for the hare — the same animal as the λαγωός of the previous sentence, called now by what it does. πολλά is adverbial, 'greatly, again and again'. τὰ εὐτελῆ, neuter, is 'the cheap things' — the creatures nobody prices highly; it takes a plural verb (φανῶσιν) where strict Attic would put a singular.

sentences.t: Ὅτι δικαιοσύνης ἐν πόλει οὔσης καὶ δικαίως πάντων δικαζόντων, καὶ οἱ εὐτελεῖς ἀταράχως βιοῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Hoti dikaiosynēs en polei ousēs kai dikaiōs pantōn dikazontōn, kai hoi euteleis atarachōs biousin.
sentences.l: That, justice being in a city and all judging justly, even the lowly live undisturbed.
sentences.i: The story shows that where justice is in a city and all judge justly, even the lowly live undisturbed.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. Two genitive absolutes stand side by side and set the condition; the second καί is 'even', marking who benefits least obviously and most.
